entry.title: What CaliciBoost taught me about molecular representations

link.title: What CaliciBoost taught me about molecular representations

entry.content:
An oral drug has to be absorbed through the intestine before it can work. Caco-2 cell permeability is a widely used in vitro proxy for this intestinal absorption, and predicting it well from structure helps prioritize compounds and saves both time and cost in ADMET screening.

Many models have been built for this task, but most studies focus on a limited set of features or a single modeling approach. In CaliciBoost (Journal of Cheminformatics, 2025), we instead compared a wide range of molecular representations systematically, to see which way of describing a molecule works best for Caco-2 permeability prediction.

The setup

We compared eight molecular representations, from fingerprints to descriptor sets to a learned embedding:

  • Fingerprints: Morgan, Avalon, ErG, MACCS
  • Descriptor sets: RDKit descriptors, PaDEL, Mordred
  • Learned embedding: CDDD

Each representation went through the same pipeline: AutoML training (AutoGluon), feature importance with permutation importance and SHAP, retraining on the top-ranked features, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. Using one pipeline for every representation kept the comparison fair.

We used two datasets that differ in scale and chemical diversity. The TDC Caco-2 benchmark has 906 compounds, with the scaffold-based split provided by TDC, so that test molecules have scaffolds not seen in training. We also curated a set of 5,481 compounds from OCHEM, about five times larger. To reduce experimental variability, we excluded measurements labeled basolateral-to-apical, measured at a pH other than 7.4, or measured at a temperature other than 37 °C, and removed duplicates.

What we found

Three things stood out to me.

Descriptor sets did best on the benchmark. On TDC, PaDEL, Mordred and RDKit descriptors gave the lowest errors. The best model, an XGBoost regressor trained on selected PaDEL descriptors, reached a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.2525 on the test set. Evaluated under the official TDC protocol over five seeds, it scored 0.2560 ± 0.006 and ranked first on the TDC Caco-2 leaderboard. The learned CDDD embedding had the highest error on TDC. Among the most influential PaDEL features were physicochemical and autocorrelation descriptors, such as the number of acidic groups (nAcid) and charge- and mass-weighted autocorrelations.

Feature selection mattered most for the largest descriptor sets. PaDEL provides 1,875 descriptors and Mordred more than 1,800. Trained on all of them, PaDEL (MAE 0.3058) and Mordred (0.3033) trailed RDKit descriptors, Morgan and Avalon. After feature selection and tuning, they moved to the top: the final PaDEL model used its 73 most important features. A smaller, well-chosen subset kept or improved accuracy while making the model easier to interpret.

The dataset changes the ranking. On the larger and more diverse OCHEM set, errors were higher for every representation, and the order shifted: RDKit descriptors did best (MAE 0.3529), while PaDEL fell to fifth. A representation that wins on one benchmark is not guaranteed to win on another, which is a good reason to test on more than one dataset before drawing conclusions.

What I take from it

For me, the main lesson was about where to spend effort. It is tempting to start with the newest architecture, but on a data-limited ADMET task, a careful choice of representation and features, combined with an AutoML model, was enough to reach the top of the benchmark. This is how I now approach other ADMET tasks: compare representations under a fixed pipeline first, then decide whether a more complex model is worth it.

The paper is open access, and the code is on GitHub.

Citation: Le HV, Ren W, Kim J, Yun Y, Park YB, Kim YJ, Han BK, Choi I, Park J-I, Yun H-y, Choi J-M. CaliciBoost: Performance-driven evaluation of molecular representations for Caco-2 permeability prediction. Journal of Cheminformatics 17, 184 (2025). doi:10.1186/s13321-025-01137-7
entry.summary: Notes on our Journal of Cheminformatics paper comparing eight molecular representations for Caco-2 permeability prediction

entry.title: Running Claude Science on Windows, then and now

link.title: Running Claude Science on Windows, then and now

entry.content:
Claude Science is Anthropic’s research application for scientists. It runs locally on your own computer rather than as a website: it sets up its own Python and R environments, connects to scientific databases and tools, and asks before it reads one of your folders or runs code. Results come back as artifacts you can open and download. It needs a Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan.

The beta: Linux and macOS only

When I first tried the beta in July 2026, it ran only on macOS and Linux. To make it easier for Windows users to try it, I tested whether the Linux version would run under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL 2). It did, and I shared the steps as a short guide on LinkedIn on 14 July.

Now: a native Windows app

Claude Science now ships a Windows installer. You download it from the product page, open it, and it installs for your user account, adds itself to the Start menu and opens in its own window. No WSL, no terminal. For most Windows users this is the way to go, and it replaces my earlier guide.

A few differences on Windows are worth knowing before you start:

  • Claude runs shell commands with PowerShell. Running git inside cells, Command Prompt scripts and changing folders in PowerShell need a one-time Windows permission. Python and R cells work without it.
  • You can only grant access to folders on local NTFS or ReFS drives, not network shares, mapped drives or most USB sticks.
  • The Model endpoints option under Settings > Compute (NVIDIA BioNeMo NIM) is not available in the Windows app.

When WSL still makes sense

The Linux version under WSL is still documented and supported. I would still pick it if:

  • my pipeline depends on Linux-only command-line tools,
  • I want Model endpoints (BioNeMo NIM), which the Windows app doesn’t offer, or
  • I want the same environment as the Linux servers I run jobs on.

Projects in the two setups are kept separately: work you create under WSL stays in WSL, and the Windows app keeps its own.

A correction to my July guide

My original guide used Ubuntu 22.04. Claude Science’s sandbox now needs bubblewrap 0.8.0 or later, and Ubuntu 22.04 ships an older version, so use Ubuntu 24.04 or newer. The short version of the current WSL setup:

# PowerShell, as Administrator
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

# Inside Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl bubblewrap socat
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install-claude-science.sh | bash
. ~/.profile
claude-science serve --port 8765 --no-browser

Open the printed http://127.0.0.1:8765 link in a Windows browser and sign in. If the link stops working, claude-science url prints a fresh one.

For the official, up-to-date steps, see Get started. My original WSL walkthrough is on LinkedIn; if you follow it, use Ubuntu 24.04 as noted above.
entry.summary: From a WSL workaround during the beta to a native Windows app, and when the Linux route still makes sense
